$comment: The declared differences between the pre-migration site and the rebuilt one.
A difference is not a failure; an undeclared difference is. Rebuilding a landing on a different
component set changes its rendered text even when not one word of copy is touched, so a comparison
that failed on any difference would force the migration to be perfect rather than honest. Every
difference therefore appears here, by route, by surface, with the value and the reason it is a
rendering change and not a copy change.
The reason text is grouped by the DECISION that moved the string rather than by the surface, so a
reader auditing the migration reads one reason per decision and can see that every string in that
decision is covered. A reason that said "rendering change" would be a placeholder, and a placeholder
reason is worse than no entry: it is a record of a decision nobody made.
Four decisions account for nearly everything here:
1. The shared chrome moved into the design system, so the header's product switcher and the
footer's groups contribute words and destinations the old hand-written copies did not.
2. The section labels carry their honesty status inside the title, so a heading that was a label
plus a separate status span is one heading, and no control affordance sits beside it.
3. The fabricated market surface is cut: a canvas of open interest generated by a sine hash, a bar
reading as a live market feed, and a nine-point retraction under it, replaced by a disclosed
diagram of the four documented capture stages. Four strings removed, one added, one disclosure
added. This is the only place on the page where a string that was a claim about a picture
rather than a fact was removed.
4. The blog's trail to the neighbouring posts says "Previous" and "Next" where the retired markup
drew arrow glyphs. A glyph is punctuation a screen reader reads as punctuation.
The route set, the content tree, every page's frontmatter and every internal destination are
unchanged, and the tool checks all four independently of this file.
The baseline this file was cut against lives outside the repository and is destroyed at the close of
the sweep. A large snapshot in a public repository is a liability, and the liability is rot rather
than secrecy.
